title: Κύων κωδωνοφορῶν
titleEn: The Dog that Wore a Bell
part: The Dog that Wore a Bell (Chambry 186 · Perry 332)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 186 (= Perry 332). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.i: There was a dog that bit on the sly.
sentences.n: λάθρᾳ is an adverbial dative, 'by stealth', and the imperfect makes it a habit rather than one bite. The whole complaint is in that adverb: this dog gave no warning before he took hold.

sentences.t: Τούτῳ δὲ ὁ δεσπότης κώδωνα ἐκρέμασεν, ὥστε πρόδηλον εἶναι τοῖς πᾶσι.
sentences.tr: Toutōi de ho despotēs kōdōna ekremasen, hōste prodēlon einai tois pasi.
sentences.l: And on this one his master hung a bell, so as for him to be plain to all.
sentences.i: So his master hung a bell on him, so that everyone would know him at once.
sentences.n: Τούτῳ is a dative of the person the thing is hung on. ὥστε with the infinitive gives the result intended. πρόδηλος is what is plain in advance, visible before it reaches you — precisely what this dog was not.

sentences.t: Οὗτος δὲ τὸν κώδωνα σείων ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ ἠλαζονεύετο.
sentences.tr: Houtos de ton kōdōna seiōn en tēi agorāi ēlazoneueto.
sentences.l: And he, shaking the bell in the market-place, gave himself airs.
sentences.n: ἀλαζονεύομαι is to play the ἀλαζών, the boaster who lays claim to what he has not got — the word the moral will come back to. The ἀγορά is the town's public square, where being seen is the entire purpose of being there.

sentences.t: Γραῦς δὲ κύων εἶπεν αὐτῷ· « Τί φαντάζῃ ; οὐ δι’ ἀρετὴν τοῦτον φορεῖς, ἀλλὰ δι’ ἔλεγχον τῆς κεκρυμμένης σου κακίας. »
sentences.tr: Graus de kyōn eipen autōi· « Ti phantazēi ; ou di’ aretēn touton phoreis, alla di’ elenchon tēs kekrymmenēs sou kakias. »
sentences.l: And an old she-dog said to him: « Why do you make a show of yourself? You do not wear this for merit, but for a proof of your hidden badness. »
sentences.i: An old she-dog said to him: « Why show yourself off? You do not wear that for merit, but as evidence of the badness you keep hidden. »
sentences.n: κύων is of either gender, and the feminine γραῦς, 'old woman', settles it: the speaker is an old she-dog. φαντάζομαι is to show oneself off, to cut a figure. διά with the accusative gives the ground of a thing, and the two grounds are set against each other. ἔλεγχος is the proof that convicts. κεκρυμμένης is a perfect passive participle — hidden, and still hidden.

sentences.t: Ὅτι οἱ τῶν ἀλαζόνων κενόδοξοι τρόποι πρόδηλοί εἰσι δηλοῦντες τὴν ἀφανῆ κακίαν.
sentences.tr: Hoti hoi tōn alazonōn kenodoxoi tropoi prodēloi eisi dēlountes tēn aphanē kakian.
sentences.l: That the vainglorious ways of braggarts are plain to all, showing up the badness that does not show.
sentences.i: The story shows that the vainglorious ways of braggarts are plain to all, and show up the badness that does not show.
sentences.n: The moral opens with a bare Ὅτι, 'that' — a subordinator with nothing above it to govern. The introducing verb is not written in the Greek: the literal line leaves the gap where the page leaves it, and the idiomatic line supplies 'the story shows'. πρόδηλοι picks up the master's purpose in hanging the bell, and ἀφανής, 'not showing', is its exact opposite: the bell makes the hidden thing audible.
